text: He begins by discussing milk and meat, saying his current concern extends beyond milk to animal products more broadly.
He says that animal feeding practices have changed worldwide over roughly the past twenty years and argues that this has created new health concerns.
He describes fish-farm by-products and low-value fish being mixed into animal feed together with grains such as corn.
He says these mixtures may be fermented for long periods and then used as feed supplements for cattle.
He claims that such feeding practices can contribute to seasonal neurological and hormonal disturbances in cattle; this is his interpretation.
He says that outbreaks sometimes labeled as infectious disease may, in his view, instead reflect changes in animal feed and resulting toxicity.
He continues by arguing that altered animal diets can lead to toxic effects and neurological symptoms in livestock.
He rejects some conventional explanations involving viruses and says that, based on his own observations, he believes the true cause is different.
He says he believes the pattern is widespread and mentions similar concerns among farmers in Egypt.
He recalls noticing neurological effects in people and says this led him to avoid meat and related animal products.
He says he also avoided animal fat and milk from cattle because of these concerns.
He then returns to milk and says his original concern was casein, a milk protein that he believes can be difficult to digest.
He says he had allowed certain cheeses because bacteria partially break down casein during fermentation.
He explains that some processed or fermented cheeses contain more fat and undergo conditions that allow bacteria to digest part of the casein.
He says the partial breakdown of casein and the higher fat content made those cheeses more acceptable within his earlier approach.
He then says his newer concern is that the meat itself may already be affected by the way animals are raised and fed.
He gives the example of rapidly growing chickens, saying modern production can increase a chick's weight dramatically within a few weeks.
He says this increase in weight does not necessarily mean the animal itself is healthy.
He contrasts modern broiler chickens with older, more active birds and says some commercially raised chickens appear unusually inactive.
He claims that some rapidly grown birds may have weak bones or serious organ problems by slaughter age; this is his allegation, not an established conclusion from the clip.
He further claims that heavy antibiotic use in feed can affect the animal's biology and behavior.
He says he believes similar practices occur with cattle, while farmers focus on the increase in size and sale weight.
He argues that the economic benefit goes to the producer while the health consequences, in his view, are passed on to consumers.
He summarizes his principle simply: remove what he considers harmful inputs and the body will function better.
He says that, in his view, many modern food products introduce unnecessary risks into the diet.
He says his role is only to point out what he believes may be harmful and that people remain free to make their own choices.
He emphasizes personal choice and says he is presenting warnings rather than forcing anyone to follow them.
He gives an example of someone eating stuffed cabbage because they were craving it.
He describes the cabbage leaf as difficult to digest and then raises concern about pesticide residues on vegetables.
He describes a person becoming overheated, shaky, short of breath, and uncomfortable after such a meal.
He says such a person might rush to the hospital and be evaluated for a cardiac problem.
He argues that severe abdominal bloating pressing on the diaphragm may sometimes be overlooked in that situation; this is his interpretation.
He recalls that stomach emptying or gastric lavage used to be performed more readily in some hospital situations before further evaluation.
He criticizes what he sees as a separation between food, medicine, and health, saying commercial interests have pushed nutrition to the side.
He says he believes nutrition and health should be considered together rather than as separate issues.
He then references Prophet Ibrahim and quotes a religious idea about God providing food and drink and healing illness.
He interprets this to mean that food can precede illness, while healing itself should not be attributed simplistically to food.
He repeats his belief that overeating contributes to disease and argues that moderation in eating supports better health.
He cites the principle, 'Eat and drink, but do not be excessive,' to support moderation.
He continues emphasizing the same religious message about eating and drinking without excess.
He criticizes modern habits of frequent eating, snacking, and consuming many different foods in a single day.
He argues that if each food creates even one problem, eating many different foods can multiply those problems; this is his rhetorical point.
He says that he sometimes goes for days without eating, presenting fasting as a way to give the body a break.
He refers to the saying 'Fast and you will be healthy' and says he sometimes avoids both food and drink for extended periods.
He says he drinks only when very thirsty and may consume very little water in a day; this is his personal practice and should not be treated as general medical advice.
He says he believes this helps his body, mood, dreams, and overall sense of well-being.
He then makes a strong claim linking chicken consumption with panic attacks and nightmares; this is his personal assertion and not established medical evidence.
He continues by claiming that people who eat chicken may have frightening dreams or become more fearful.
He says he has repeated this claim for years and presents it as something he is willing to argue strongly.
He gives an example involving Iranians and chicken consumption to support his view, but this is an unsupported generalization.
He ends by repeating his belief that eating chicken is linked with fearfulness.
